newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAFRICA RESERVE BANK SEES LOWER MONEY MKT SHORTAGE.
newsitem.headline: SAFRICA RESERVE BANK SEES LOWER MONEY MKT SHORTAGE.

text.p: South Africa's money market shortage could decline substantially after the maturity of government's R119 gilt on Friday, Roelf du Plooy, assistant general manager of the Reserve Bank's money and capital markets division said on Wednesday.

The shortage has risen to the 9.6 billion rand ($2.1 billion) level this week owing mainly to the maturing of Reserve Bank dollar forward contracts this month and a mismatch in government flows last weekend. It began the month at 7.910 billion rand.
But du Plooy said the shortage could be expected to decline from its current levels as the month progressed.

"There will be an expansionary impact on liquidity which could result in a substantially lower shortage as the month progresses," du Plooy said, adding that it was difficult to give any indication of the magnitude of the fall.

He said government was going to use the receipts of the R119s held in the Corporation for Public Deposits' (CPD) portfolio to service the redemption of R119s still in the market and interest payments later in the month.

Some 8.5 billion rand is outstanding on the R119 stock, while semi-annual coupon payments of around 7.5 billion rand are due on a variety of government stocks -- mainly the benchmark R150 and R153 on September 1.
A spokesperson at the CPD, which serves as a repository for public sector funds, told Reuters it currently held a nominal amount of 2.3 billion rand of R119 stock.

Du Plooy said the central bank could use various unspecified counter-actions against the inflow into the market, but added that there was sufficient cash on both the exchequer and Tax and Loan accounts -- held at commercial banks -- to service the redemption and interest payments.
Senior money market traders said the current squeeze on liquidity had little impact on short-term rates.
"At the moment there is no pressure. The (rates) are marking time right now," one senior trader said.
Three-month NCDs were quoted unchanged at between 15.40 to 15.50 percent offered, while the 90-day BA rate was also unchanged at 14.90 to 14.95 percent.
"At this stage we haven't seen any real pressure on the shorter end of the market," another senior trader said, "and until we get an interest rate move I don't expect much movement," he said.
He added that the current level of short-term rates had fully discounted a one percentage point interest rate cut in September.
Bank rate -- the official lending rate which currently stands at 17 percent -- was last hiked by one percentage point in November last year.
Economists expect at least one and possibly two 100 basis point reductions by year-end.
